decision.explanation: Using sin(A)sin(B) = [cos(A−B)−cos(A+B)]/2, the integrand is [cos(9x)−cos(11x)]/2. Integrating gives sin(9x)/18−sin(11x)/22+C, which is option d.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(10x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(10x-x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(10x+x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(11x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(10x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(11x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)-\frac{1}{22}\operatorname{sin}⁡(11x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(13x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(13x-5x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(13x+5x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(18x)).\end{aligned}

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x+5x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x-5x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(12x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(7x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(12x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{24}\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x)-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

content.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x+5x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x-5x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(12x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(7x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(12x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{24}\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x)-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.
